title: File Handling & Error Handling
description: Read and write files safely, and handle errors gracefully with try/except

lessons.title: Reading Files
lessons.description: Open and read text files safely

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Open a file with `with`, read it fully or line by line.

sections.title: 📖 Opening Files with `with`
sections.content:
Always use `with` — it automatically closes the file, even if an error occurs.

```python
with open("data.txt", "r") as f:
    content = f.read()      # whole file as one string

with open("data.txt", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()   # list of lines

with open("data.txt", "r") as f:
    for line in f:           # memory-efficient line-by-line
        print(line.strip())
```

sections.title: 🗂️ File Modes
sections.content:
• `'r'` — read (default)
• `'w'` — write (overwrites existing content!)
• `'a'` — append (adds to the end)
• `'r+'` — read and write

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting `.strip()` and getting extra `\n` characters at the end of each line when reading line by line.

questions.question: Why use `with open(...) as f:`?
options: It automatically closes the file, even on errors
questions.explanation: The context manager guarantees cleanup.

questions.question: What does `f.read()` return?
options: The entire file contents as one string
questions.explanation: read() slurps everything into a single string.

questions.question: What does `f.readlines()` return?
options: A list of lines (with newline characters)
questions.explanation: Each element is a line, including its trailing \n.

questions.question: What mode overwrites a file's existing content?
questions.explanation: Write mode truncates the file before writing.

questions.question: What mode appends to a file without erasing it?
questions.explanation: Append mode adds new content at the end.

questions.question: Iterating `for line in f:` is efficient because...
options: It reads one line at a time instead of loading the whole file
It's the only way to read files
questions.explanation: This avoids loading huge files entirely into memory.

questions.question: Why might `line.strip()` be needed when printing lines?
options: To remove the trailing newline character
questions.explanation: Lines from a file usually include a trailing \n.

questions.question: What is the default mode of `open()`?
questions.explanation: If you omit the mode argument, it defaults to read.

lessons.title: Writing Files
lessons.description: Create and write to text files

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Write and append text to files using write() and writelines().

sections.title: ✍️ Writing Text
sections.content:
```python
with open("output.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Hello, file!\n")
    f.write("Second line\n")

with open("output.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Appended line\n")
```

sections.title: 📋 Writing Multiple Lines
sections.content:
```python
lines = ["line1\n", "line2\n", "line3\n"]
with open("output.txt", "w") as f:
    f.writelines(lines)
```

Note: `writelines()` does NOT add newlines for you — include `\n` in each string yourself.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Using mode `'w'` when you meant `'a'`, accidentally erasing an existing file's content.

questions.question: What does `f.write("text")` do?
options: Writes the string to the file (no automatic newline)
questions.explanation: write() does not add \n automatically — you must include it.

questions.question: What's the risk of using mode 'w' on an existing file?
options: It erases the existing content first
questions.explanation: 'w' truncates the file before writing new content.

questions.question: What does `writelines(lines)` require for proper line breaks?
options: Each string in the list must already include \n
questions.explanation: writelines() concatenates strings exactly as given.

questions.question: Which mode adds text to the end of a file without erasing it?
questions.explanation: Append mode preserves existing content.

questions.question: What is the safe way to write to a file?
questions.explanation: with ensures the file is properly closed after writing.

questions.question: If you want to guarantee you don't overwrite an existing file, which mode raises an error if the file exists?
questions.explanation: 'x' mode fails if the file already exists.

questions.question: What does the file look like after two `f.write()` calls without `\n`?
options: Both strings joined with no line break
Each on its own line automatically
Only the last write is kept
questions.explanation: write() doesn't insert separators between calls.

questions.question: Which is correct for writing a list of lines with breaks?
questions.explanation: You must add the newline character yourself before calling writelines().

lessons.title: try / except / finally
lessons.description: Handle errors gracefully instead of crashing

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Catch specific exceptions, use else/finally, and understand why bare except is risky.

sections.title: 🛡️ Basic try/except
🧩 else and finally
Common mistakes
sections.content: Using a bare `except:` that catches everything — including typos and Ctrl+C — instead of naming the specific exception you expect.

questions.question: What does `except ZeroDivisionError:` catch?
questions.explanation: Naming a specific exception type limits what's caught.

questions.question: When does the `else` block in try/except run?
questions.explanation: else runs when the try block completes without raising.

questions.question: When does `finally` run?
options: Always, whether or not an exception occurred
questions.explanation: finally is for guaranteed cleanup code.

questions.question: Why is a bare `except:` discouraged?
options: It silently catches all errors, hiding bugs
questions.explanation: Catching everything can mask real problems, including typos.

questions.question: What does `except ValueError as e:` let you do?
options: Access details of the exception via e
questions.explanation: The `as e` binds the exception object for inspection.

questions.question: What happens if no matching except block exists for a raised exception?
options: It propagates up and can crash the program
questions.explanation: Unhandled exceptions bubble up the call stack.

questions.question: Which exception is raised by `int("abc")`?
questions.explanation: Converting a non-numeric string raises ValueError.

questions.question: Is it good practice to catch specific exceptions rather than everything?
questions.explanation: Specific exceptions communicate intent and avoid masking bugs.

lessons.title: Raising & Custom Exceptions
lessons.description: Signal errors intentionally and define your own exception types

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Raise built-in exceptions with messages and define a simple custom exception class.

sections.title: 🚨 Raising Exceptions
sections.content:
Use `raise` to signal that something has gone wrong.

```python
def withdraw(balance, amount):
    if amount > balance:
        raise ValueError("Insufficient funds")
    return balance - amount

withdraw(100, 200)   # raises ValueError: Insufficient funds
```

sections.title: 🏷️ Custom Exceptions
Common mistakes
sections.content: Raising a generic `Exception` for everything — specific or custom exception types make error handling much more precise for callers.

questions.question: What does `raise ValueError("msg")` do?
options: Immediately signals an error with that message
questions.explanation: raise interrupts normal flow to signal the exception.

questions.question: How do you define a custom exception?
questions.explanation: Custom exceptions subclass Exception (or a more specific built-in).

questions.question: Why create custom exceptions?
options: To give callers precise, meaningful error types to catch
questions.explanation: Specific exception types make error handling clearer for callers.

questions.question: What is `Exception` in Python?
options: The base class most exceptions derive from
questions.explanation: Most custom and built-in exceptions inherit from Exception.

questions.question: What does `pass` inside a custom exception class body do?
options: Adds no extra behavior beyond the base class
Prevents the exception from being raised
questions.explanation: pass is a placeholder when there's nothing extra to add.

questions.question: Can you catch a custom exception like a built-in one?
options: No, custom exceptions can't be caught
questions.explanation: Custom exceptions work with try/except exactly like built-ins.

questions.question: What happens if you `raise` an exception that's never caught?
options: The program terminates with a traceback
questions.explanation: Uncaught exceptions propagate up and crash the program with a traceback.

questions.question: Which is more informative for callers: raising `Exception` or a custom `InsufficientFundsError`?
questions.explanation: Specific exception types communicate the exact problem.

lessons.title: Working with CSV & JSON Files
lessons.description: Read and write common structured data formats

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Load and save data using the csv and json standard library modules.

sections.title: 📊 CSV Files
sections.content:
```python
import csv

with open("data.csv", "r") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    for row in reader:
        print(row)   # each row is a list of strings

with open("data.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["name", "age"])
    writer.writerow(["Alice", 30])
```

`csv.DictReader`/`DictWriter` work with dictionaries instead of lists, using the header row as keys.

sections.title: 🧾 JSON Files
sections.content:
JSON maps naturally to Python dicts and lists.

```python
import json

data = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}

# Write
with open("data.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(data, f)

# Read
with open("data.json", "r") as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)

# String <-> object without a file
json.dumps(data)          # '{"name": "Alice", "age": 30}'
json.loads('{"x": 1}')    # {'x': 1}
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Mixing up `json.dump`/`load` (file objects) with `json.dumps`/`loads` (strings) — the 's' versions work on strings, not files.

questions.question: Which module reads/writes JSON in Python?
questions.explanation: The json module handles encoding/decoding.

questions.question: What does `json.dumps(data)` return?
questions.explanation: The 's' suffix means it works with strings, not files.

questions.question: What does `json.load(f)` do?
options: Reads JSON from a file object into a Python object
questions.explanation: load() (no 's') reads directly from an open file.

questions.question: What does `csv.reader(f)` yield per row?
questions.explanation: Each row from csv.reader is a list of strings.

questions.question: What's the advantage of `csv.DictReader`?
options: Rows come back as dicts keyed by the header row
questions.explanation: DictReader uses the first row as field names automatically.

questions.question: When opening a CSV file for writing on Windows, what avoids extra blank lines?
questions.explanation: newline="" prevents the csv module from adding extra line endings.

questions.question: What does `json.loads('{"x": 1}')` return?
questions.explanation: loads() parses a JSON string into Python objects.

questions.question: Which pair works with strings, not files?
questions.explanation: The 's' functions (dumps, loads) are the string variants.
